newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Delta rocket explodes on takeoff.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Delta rocket explodes on takeoff.

text.p: An unmanned Delta II rocket carrying a $40 million U.S. Air Force navigational satellite exploded on Friday just after blastoff, scattering flaming debris and sending billowing smoke for miles.

About 13 seconds after the 11:28 a.m. EST (1628 GMT) liftoff from Cape Canaveral Air Station, a system designed to detect problems with the rocket triggered its destruction, Air Force Brigadier Gen. Robert Hinson, wing commander of the 45th Space Wing, said.

"At T plus 13 seconds there was a self destruct initiated, which resulted in the total destruction of the Delta and its payload," he said. That, in turn, prompted Air Force flight safety personnel to send a precautionary destruct signal to minimize danger from the falling of any large fragments to the ground.
He declined to speculate about what might have caused the explosion and said the Air Force had formed an early investigation team, which would be replaced by a formal board of inquiry later.
"The loss of any launch vehicle is catastrophic to us. We rely on 100 percent launch capability," Hinson said.

The Delta rocket launch program began in the late 1950s when NASA contracted McDonnell Douglas to modify its Thor ballistic missile as a space launcher. Today it is a mainstay of the U.S. unmanned space fleet.
Last year NASA entrusted the rocket with the launch of two Mars probes, which spearhead NASA's return to the Red Planet, an effort costing hundreds of millions of dollars.

This year the Delta is slated to launch several satellites for the Iridium project, a web of 66 low-orbit satellites that will ring the Earth, providing virtually worldwide wireless communications. Motorola has about a 25 percent stake in the international consortium.

A spokesman for Iridium LLC said Friday's explosion would delay the launch that had been planned for Monday. It is industry practice not to launch another rocket after an explosion until the investigation produces results.
A Delta rocket last exploded in May 1986.
Witnesses said the explosion, which occurred just 1,589 feet (530 meters) above the launch pad, was spectacular.

"I heard the main explosion and after that I heard three, four, more minor explosions and more smoke and more fireballs, and that's basically it," said Kurt Ronstrom, a freelance photographer who was photographing the blastoff about two miles (3.2 km) from the launch pad.

Photographers and reporters about a mile (1.6 km) from the launch pad had to dive for cover when the blast occurred. They had been routinely advised beforehand that in the unlikely event of an explosion they might be at risk.

The rocket was carrying a NAVSTAR Block IIR satellite built by Lockheed Martin Corp, the first of a new generation of U.S. Air Force Global Positioning System satellites. The satellites provide navigation information to U.S. military troops, aircraft, submarines and ships around the world. They also are used by civilians, such as boaters and truckers and pilots, to pinpoint their locations.
A spokesman for Boeing Co. said a division of his company had built the engine of the Delta II rocket that blew up.
On television tape, the explosion seemed to originate at the base of the Delta II, where nine solid-fueled rockets were located, as well as the liquid-fueled main engine.

Television news footage showed sparks showering the launch pad seconds after takeoff. Half an hour later witnesses said smoke was continuing to billow from the pad, and a cloud from the blast moved down the coast for two hours.
